Business.title: National museums to stay free to all visitors, government says
Business.text:
Overseas visitors will not be charged to enter England's national museums after ministers decided against changing the universal free admission policy.

It comes after months of discussions between the government, museums, the tourism sector and local leaders to examine whether making tourists from abroad pay could boost the institutions' finances.

In March, the government said it would explore charging international visitors to enter national museums as it looks for ways to tackle funding pressures.

But the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has now said this could deter domestic visitors and that any benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector.

The UK's 15 national museums, including 12 in London, have been free for all to enter since 2001.

But a review published last year by former Labour minister Baroness Margaret Hodge suggested that a charging model for international tourists "would align the UK with other countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore".

On Tuesday, DCMS confirmed free admission to these museums would remain in place for everyone.

"The government believes that charging overseas visitors could deter domestic visitors and that the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector and therefore will not introduce charges for overseas visitors," a spokesperson said.

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Our museums are the places that light up the world.

"That's why they must be free, forever, for everyone to access."

The DCMS said national museums contribute more than £1bn a year to the economy and attract visitors from around the world, with the Natural History Museum and the British Museum drawing 7.1 million and 6.4 million visitors respectively in 2025.

The Natural History Museum's director Dr Doug Gurr said although his museum would have benefitted from charging, the sector would have lost out overall.

"Free museums aren't a cost to the economy - they're a key reason the economy benefits from tourism in the first place," he said.

"So, we're delighted to remain free but given the visitors we bring there's a strong case for reinvesting a share of any tourism revenues in the institutions that help attract them."

Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, said: "When the British Museum was founded as the world's first public national museum in 1753 it was to be free for 'all persons'.

"So, we are delighted by the government's announcement that free entry for all will be maintained.

"This will allow everyone to enjoy and have access to our great museums across the nation as one of the things this country does so brilliantly."

The government also pointed to £760m in funding for museums through its £1.5bn Arts Everywhere Fund, as well as £600m in infrastructure funding for national museums.

It said the £13.6m museum transformation programme would help organisations move towards more sustainable business models, while ministers would work with the Arts Council and the sector on a long-term strategic plan for museums, with further details to be announced.

Sports.title: Manchester City charges: Premier League confirms club guilty of all charges related to financial rule breaches
Sports.text:
Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of its commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m, the Premier League says.

The League confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".

The club continues to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

News broke last week that City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, but on Tuesday the Premier League published a redacted version of the commission's report.

The commission's report said the charges "concerned well over 100 alleged individual breaches of Premier League Rules across four broad charge categories".

It also found the club guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.

The sham commercial deals were described as being part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

City recorded £360m in sponsor fees in the three seasons they won the Premier League - 2011-12, 2013-14, and 2017-18. Only £43m of it was legitimate - the rest came from their owners and was disguised.

"The relevant sponsorship agreements were found to be shams, or at minimum did not reflect their economic substance," the commission said.

It also describes "deliberate or reckless conduct intended to circumvent the Premier League rules" and that the "sham" scheme devised by City allowed the club "to avoid recording what would otherwise have been the largest single-season loss in Premier League history in 2009-10".

The commission highlighted the scale of evidence it had to consider by pointing out that the index alone ran to more than 750 pages, while the core bundle of documents "ran to many tens of thousands of pages".

City are owned by the Abu Dhabi United Group, who took over the club in 2008 and are referred to as "ADUG" in the commission's report.

Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, said: "The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

"It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

"It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously."

The Premier League also said that City's sanction "will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission".

The League's rules state that the hearing must remain private and confidential.

Lisa Nandy MP, the Culture, Media & Sport secretary, told the BBC: "It's incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark.

"This is causing a lot of concern for Man City fans and all fans of Premier League football."

In its own statement, the club said: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Sports.title: UK diesel price hits all-time high, the RAC says
Sports.text:
Diesel prices have hit an all-time high of 199.33p per litre, according to the RAC motoring organisation, as the war in the Middle East continues to push up the cost of fuel.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.23p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

The cost of diesel has now risen by 59p a litre, or just under 40%, since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted at the end of February. The previous record was 199.09p in June 2022 following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The increase means the cost of filling an average family car with diesel is now £110, £31 more than at the start of the conflict.

Petrol prices are now 41p per litre more than at the start of the conflict, but still well below a 2022 peak.

The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers.

The Chancellor said on Monday that the the "place" and "time" for the government to deal with questions around rising petrol and diesel prices and fuel duty is next month's Budget.

John Healey told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm acutely concerned and conscious about how hard it is for families. I see that at the pumps myself.

"We can't remove the cost of living pressures, we can't remove the prices that people are having to pay, but where we can we will act and we will give people just a bit of breathing space, and the same goes for the cost to business."

Simon Williams, the RAC's head of policy, said record diesel prices "spell pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans".

"Undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers," he said. Williams said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days".

The price of Brent crude, a benchmark for global oil used to make petrol, diesel and other fuel products, rose over the weekend and is now hovering at around $108 per barrel. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has also implemented an export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply.

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney says Manchester United do not deserve Manchester City titles
Sports.text:
Wayne Rooney says his former club Manchester United do not deserve to be awarded Premier League titles if rivals Manchester City are stripped of them for breaching financial rules.

City have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.

The financial charges relate to the period from 2009-10 to 2017-18, while they were also accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between December 2018 to February 2023.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City plan to appeal against the decision.

One possible punishment could be the club being stripped of top-flight titles. They have won the Premier League eight times since Sheikh Mansour's takeover in 2009, three of which were in the period when they were accused of breaking financial rules.

Rooney was part of the United side that finished runners-up to City in 2011-2012 but does not want to be awarded the title retrospectively.

Speaking on the Stick to United podcast,, external he said: "I wouldn't feel comfortable about accepting another Premier League medal if I'm being honest, because I don't think we deserve it. We didn't do enough that season to win the league.

"I'm thinking as their players, they're there doing everything they can to win the Premier League title and in their minds they've done it.

"And, if those players have got no understanding of what's going on above them, then if that happened to me - if all of a sudden Manchester United have been doing the same and I'm getting my Premier League medals taken away from me - I'd be absolutely devastated.

"They might take them away but I wouldn't want it because I don't feel as a team we deserved it that year because we obviously didn't finish first."

Rooney's former United team-mates Rio Ferdinand and David de Gea both posted on social media after news of the guilty verdict emerged on Friday, suggesting they should be awarded retrospective title wins.

And former Stoke City boss Tony Pulis said he felt "cheated" after his side were beaten by the Blues in the 2011 FA Cup final.

"When I've heard of ex-team-mates and people saying, 'we've won another medal', I'm happy with the five I've won," said Rooney.

"I wouldn't want this one just sat there... 15 years later or whatever it was you get a medal because City cheated. I wouldn't feel comfortable.

"The question is, would I want to receive that medal for finishing second? No.

"Some players might. I just wouldn't feel comfortable for accepting a Premier League medal for finishing second."

While Rooney is against titles being taken away from City, he does believe they should be relegated.

"I do think we're going to see City getting relegated," said the 40-year-old. "However that happens I don't know but I think we're going to see them get relegated."

Rooney added: "I'd put them in the lowest league they can go in and then put restrictions on them in terms of how much money they can spend for the next three or four seasons.

"If you're just putting them in the Championship, and I get that's a massive punishment, they're going to come back up. Where, I feel if they have got restrictions... League Two, whatever... that could be very difficult for them.

"For instance, if they got a 20-point deduction for the next three years then players won't want to stay there. If it's Championship for a season, you could talk players round.

"I'd go as big as I can really."

Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino, meanwhile, says "we have lived through a period of deception".

Pochettino managed three clubs in the Premier League during the period covering City's charges, with the 54-year-old spending 15 months at Southampton, five years at Tottenham and a single season with Chelsea.

"Whatever punishment [they choose], it's impossible to turn back time," said Pochettino.

"It's done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules and some didn't.

"Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn't come for a lot of years] - what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard.

"It is a huge sadness. We get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened.

"We went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception."

Earlier this month, Pochettino said Chelsea should be stripped of the 2016-17 Premier League title after being found guilty of historical rule breaches and that it should be "awarded" to his Tottenham side, who finished runners-up.

Sources have told BBC Sport that other top flight clubs are seeking legal advice over possible compensation claims following the decision against City.

City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation.

The club were referred to an independent commission. A behind-closed-doors hearing began in September 2024 and ran for about 12 weeks.

"Where were the controls?" said Pochettino on City being found guilty. "That's what gets my attention. Where were the controls?

"If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham - I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months.

"I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer].

"Tottenham was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of the Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the [Premier League financial controls]?

"They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange."

On Tuesday, La Liga president Javier Tebas said he agreed with Pochettino and believes City should face the most severe sanctions possible after an "era of disappointment".

"In my opinion, the most severe sanction provided for under the Premier League regulations should be applied," Tebas, 64, told BBC Sport at a summit in London hosted by global players' union Fifapro.

"Given the number of years involved, the repeated breaches, the denial and the lack of cooperation, the most severe sanction allowed under the Premier League rules is what should be imposed, although I do not know exactly what that sanction would be."

On Tuesday, La Liga president Javier Tebas said he agreed with Pochettino's verdict and added: "In my opinion, the most severe sanction provided for under the Premier League regulations should be applied.

"Given the number of years involved, the repeated breaches, the denial and the lack of co-operation, the most severe sanction allowed under the Premier League rules is what should be imposed, although I do not know exactly what that sanction would be," Tebas, 64, told BBC Sport at a summit in London hosted by global players' union Fifapro.

The Spaniard added that he had been raising concerns about City's conduct for "many years".

Sports.title: Rui Pinto: The hacker who tried to take down Manchester City
Sports.text:
Mention Rui Pinto's name to Manchester City fans outside Etihad Stadium, and you mostly get blank faces.

But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work.

Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City.

Through his website Football Leaks, he published a cache of confidential club documents, including internal emails about sponsorship deals and payments.

That ultimately led to the Premier League charges for breaching of financial rules and Friday's news that the club had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 counts.

For some, 37-year-old Pinto is no more than a criminal who stole information with sinister intentions.

To others, though, he is a bastion of truth who has shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.

BBC Sport has been on a journey across Europe to find out more about the mysterious figure who was the catalyst for so much controversy.

We spoke to one of Pinto's former teachers, a Portuguese politician fighting for him to be protected as a whistleblower, journalists who published the leaks, and a former financial adviser at Manchester City.

And we sat just a few feet from Pinto in the latest of his court cases.

With his cherubic face and spiky hair, Pinto is instantly recognisable. And it seems he hasn't changed.

It is how Mario Falcao, his former geography teacher, remembers him.

In a small courtyard garden in Portugal, we got a glimpse of what Pinto was like as a boy.

"Rui was a perfectly normal pupil. He was nice, with his spiky hair, he was quite sociable but not extrovert," Falcao said.

"He had a good relationship with the teachers, although he did miss these classes quite often. His father was always on top of things, so in the end he passed quite easily."

Did he spot a strong interest in computers in a young Pinto?

"Certainly he was very good in computers. All the work that he did for various courses were very good, when he put his mind to it," his former teacher explained.

The now-retired Falcao speaks fondly of Pinto, who he says behaved just like his friends and would "go to the gym, go to McDonald's".

Pinto had a modest upbringing. He grew up in an area called Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the Douro River from Porto, Portugal's second-largest city. We visited the road where he used to live, which featured tile-fronted houses with terracotta roofs.

His school, Escola Secundaria Almeida Garrett, was well-regarded and was known by locals as 'the university'.

His father, Francisco, worked in a shoe factory and later as an antiques dealer. His mother had died when he was 11.

Falcao said he never predicted what was to come of his former pupil.

"We were very surprised," he said of the moment Pinto was named as the founder of Football Leaks in 2019.

"We weren't imagining anything like this could happen, that he could have problems with justice.

"I certainly wouldn't wish him and his family to be in this situation. Perhaps it was a question of the excesses of youth, his ability with computers, and maybe an excess of club-ism."

"So, you know, the fact that he supported FC Porto prompted him to commit some acts, but maybe he also felt the need for justice that young people very often do feel."

Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football".

Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John".

"It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important."

Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums.

"We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela.

"You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion."

It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted.

The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto.

Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar.

Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him.

It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen.

Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team.

"In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said.

"If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work.

"It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context and you can see if there's any reliability issues.

"We always need to make sure that it's authentic material and whenever we publish something about it, it needs to be in the public interest to start writing."

Winterbach finally met Pinto in person in 2019, when he was being held in prison in Lisbon awaiting his trial. He conducted another interview with Pinto in witness protection, in a secret location with high security, describing the arrangements for getting there as being "like a Hollywood movie".

He said: "Rui Pinto is not very tall. He has very distinctive hair, like spiky hair. He usually has red cheeks and he's a youthful, cheeky, funny character. He's friendly and warm when you meet him.

"He's a very impressive character, he's very focused, he's very concentrated. He's very, very intelligent. He's very idealistic about the topics that he uncovered.

"He's one of the most important whistleblowers that we have in Europe or maybe the world."

In all, Pinto provided more than three terabytes - equivalent to about 3,000 copies of the Encyclopedia Britannica - of information to Der Spiegel and other outlets in the European Investigative Collaborations consortium.

We encountered stark contrasts in perceptions of Pinto wherever we went.

Former Portuguese politician and diplomat Ana Gomes has also met Pinto in prison and testified on his behalf at one of his trials. She is firmly of the view that he deserves to be protected, not prosecuted.

"What he has exposed is very important. In Portugal, definitely he is by far the most important whistleblower," the former Member of the European Parliament told us in Lisbon.

"He should be made an ally of our judicial and criminal investigative authorities. He has helped the authorities of other European countries in going after the corrupt and the criminals, instead of being the subject of this judicial prosecution by the choice of our public prosecutors."

When asked what she would say to Manchester City, who had their emails hacked by him, her answer is blunt.

"I couldn't care less. If they have nothing to hide, what's their problem?"

Jose Carlos Freitas, a retired journalist, said Gomes's sympathetic view is not a widely held one.

"For the majority of the people, they look at him as a thief," he said. "For some people, he is a kind of hero, a Robin Hood, you can say because he was exposing the dark side of the business of so many clubs, but unfortunately for the majority of the people, he is not a good person."

Varela is on the fence. "Nowadays, I think I put him in the middle [between whistleblower and criminal hacker] because he got the information illegally. But he gave us, all of us, a view, a dark view of European football, so he did a job to the society illegally."

Wherever you sit in the debate, he has faced serious consequences for what he did. As Winterbach puts it, Pinto "has powerful enemies through the work that he has done".

For the past six years, Pinto's life has been far from normal.

Having been arrested in Hungary in 2019, he was extradited to Portugal and has at various points been in solitary confinement, under house arrest and in witness protection.

Following his first trial in Portugal, in 2023 he received a four-year suspended sentence having been found guilty of attempted extortion, illegal access to data and breach of correspondence.

A separate trial in France resulted in a six-month suspended prison sentence a few months later.

And in January last year, Pinto's latest trial began in Lisbon. The opening day at the Central Criminal Court encapsulated the realities of his life and the difference in opinions of him.

Pinto arrived with members of his witness protection team, two of whom stayed in the courtroom throughout the hearing, along with an armed police presence.

He was dressed casually in a blue, long-sleeved top, jeans and brown boots, and had his distinctive spiky hair and some facial hair. He was fairly expressionless throughout, aside from the occasional shrug of the shoulders or glance at his team.

We sat just a few feet from him, as he conversed with his legal team in hushed tones and spoke to the judge purely to confirm details like his name and age. When asked for his address, he said he could not give this for security reasons.

Local journalist Miguel Dantas explained the security arrangements were scaled back compared with the first trial, when he wore a bulletproof jacket and there were snipers on the roof.

Rui Patricio, the lawyer representing Benfica, told the court Pinto was "no more, no less than a burglar", that he had obtained the information by "illegal and condemnable methods" and that the ends did not justify the means.

Outside court, Patricio added: "Our argument is very, very simple. He's a hacker, period, just like that. What he did is not allowed - it's a crime and there are no excuses. It's very, very simple. Very, very straightforward."

In his statement in court, Francisco Texeira da Mota, representing Pinto, accepted that his client was "not a hero and not a saint" but said he had brought "advantages for society".

The impact of Football Leaks is still being felt a decade on.

The Premier League's case against Manchester City has been one of unprecedented scale and significance.

From speaking to his legal team after the court hearing, it became clear Pinto has been closely monitoring that case from witness protection since the Premier League brought the charges in February 2023.

Asked if the outcome mattered, Texeira da Mota said: "I think it's important for him because it's very difficult to be like he is, living a very difficult life, more or less hiding, because he made some revelations, he whistle-blowed lots of important things, namely about Manchester City.

"So it would be important for him to feel vindicated that it was useful, that something happened, because what of what he said."

Speaking before the announcement of the decision in the City case, Stefan Borson, a former financial adviser to Manchester City, said: "I think for City, really, the whole of the Sheikh Mansour era is at stake if the core allegations are proven against the club.

"I think the consequences could be very far reaching for the club, and it would be a very difficult thing for them to deal with.

"Over time, clearly there would have to be some kind of reset. I think in many ways the Premier League is a loser either way."

Borson's view was that Pinto should not be seen as "some kind of warrior for freedom".

He said: "We know that what he carried out was a criminal act and he's been prosecuted for it.

"We also know that hackers of that nature do try and reframe themselves as part of the defence process as purveyors of freedom of speech. But, once those documents are in the public domain, then I think it's for the authorities to act."

For some, Rui Pinto is a criminal hacker who stole information with sinister intentions. To others he is a heroic whistleblower who shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.

What is undeniable is that one Portuguese man on his computer in Budapest has had a seismic impact on global football.

But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work. Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City. Sports.title: Manchester City charges: What punishment could club face after Premier League verdict and will they appeal?
Sports.text:
If you had the impression that the saga over Manchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again.

Two years since the hearing began, the Premier League has confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of its financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and would pursue "appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now.

City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion.

The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who strongly refute the accusations.

When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole.

And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation.

Enzo Maresca's side go to Liverpool on 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless?

Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing.

Deciding the punishment should be quicker than ascertaining guilt, but nothing is certain in this case.

As the charges have been denied, it will have to go to a sanction hearing convened by the independent panel.

At the hearing, everything will be on the table. Fines, points deductions and even demotion.

This differs from Chelsea's case earlier this year, as the Stamford Bridge club self-reported and admitted guilt. That allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League and reach a sanctioning agreement.

The panel will have to comb through the hundreds of pages of evidence and determine the punishment.

Remember, Everton were docked six points, reduced from 10 on appeal, and then two points in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR). Nottingham Forest were deducted four points.

These were considered to be minor breaches, while City faced seven separate charges on PSR breaches in the Premier League alone, as well as a further five related to Uefa competitions.

This aspect alone suggests a large points penalty.

That is before you get into the findings that the club arranged "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs", equating to roughly £830m of extra revenue from sponsorship deals.

Take all this into account, and it places an asterisk against the Premier League between 2009 and 2018.

Chelsea and Manchester City, two of the competition's most successful clubs, have been part of that. While Chelsea admitted effectively cheating, City have been found guilty. They got around the financial rules to put them in a position to be able to sign more expensive players than their finances should have permitted.

And if this season passes with no decision on the sanction while it is known City were guilty of the majority of counts, what does that mean for the integrity of the competition?

Could a penalty be backdated to this season when finally awarded? Unlikely.

So what if Manchester City win the league?

Coventry are third from bottom right now. What if they finish in that position, are relegated, but would have stayed up had City's punishment come this season?

This inertia is terrible news for the Premier League as a competition.

There's a strong argument that a sanctioning agreement is the cleanest way out of this.

But that may not be palatable to the league as they would have to negotiate with City, who would presumably want a lesser punishment.

The usual process when any points penalty is handed down is that it is applied immediately, subject to appeal.

It could be a points deduction so large that it is effectively a relegation.

Alternatively, if City's membership of the Premier League was revoked, it is unclear how that might be applied mid-season.

It could also be that the punishment is a huge fine, although that would seem unlikely given points deductions to other clubs.

The question would be how soon we hear, and how long after the appeal is heard.

While there are timelines for the appeal process within the Premier League regulations, it is unclear whether they would directly apply here.

City have until Friday to appeal.

Usually, the league asks for an expedited process from the independent arbitration company which handles disciplinary cases.

But, as ever in this case, the complexities indicate this is not straightforward.

There is the chance, though slim, that the punishment is only applied to the league table after the appeal.

That would surely lead to protests from impacted teams this season, who will demand it should, as usual, come into effect immediately.

For the integrity of the Premier League, so all clubs know what they are playing for, this would need to happen sooner rather than later.

Last season, a points deduction for West Bromwich Albion related to breaches of profit and sustainability regulations was not announced until 24 April.

While ultimately they stayed in the Championship, it plunged them back into a relegation fight when they thought they were safe. It also gave some hope to the teams in the relegation zone.

The Premier League does not want this to drag on until the penultimate month of the season, but nothing is guaranteed in this story.

In this scenario, let's not forget City could also win their appeal, like they did over a two-year Champions League ban handed down by Uefa in July 2020.

However, unlike with Uefa, City would not be able to take this case to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

While this would be celebrated at Etihad Stadium it would likely not be the end of the acrimony over the case.

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation from Manchester City over the case.

One source, who held a senior executive position at two Premier League sides, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims against Manchester City.

Another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could even be centralised by the league.

Premier League rules allow clubs to seek legal action against each other for compensation.

In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35m after they broke PSR over a three-year period.

Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.

Everton are appealing, with sources previously saying they would "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to the Manchester City case.

There is uncertainty over a statute of limitations, which would set a cut-off point for claims.

Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham Hotspur reportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation two years ago.

This is not just about Manchester United (twice) and Liverpool, who finished as runners-up to City in their title-winning seasons.

It is about those clubs who just missed out on the Champions League, or failed to make Europe, or even those who were relegated.

And it could even result in claims over the prize money for each Premier League place, or the potential commercial earnings lost by rival clubs.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport it would be considered a "denial of an opportunity" by complainants.

Maguire explained that the "statute of limitations is not referenced" in the Premier League's traditional handbook, though that could be subject to a legal challenge from City.

But what of the compensation? Just looking at Champions League qualifying could bring huge financial claims.

"The Champions League in those days was worth a minimum of £30m," Maguire said. "I think by the time we got to 2018, it was probably worth £60m or £70m, and that's in prize money.

"On top of that, you could claim for loss of gate receipts, loss of sponsor bonuses. This is highly unlikely, but it's certainly being discussed.

"Players get bonuses for qualifying for the Champions League. Those bonuses, if you talk to people connected to the elite clubs, are normally in the region of 25%.

"An average salary in those days would probably, if you go back to 2012, be in the region of £80,000 or £90,000 a week. Twenty-five percent of that is four or five million pounds a year. That's how the issues stack up."

Points deductions, fines, and compensation claims.

This is an extremely messy situation for the Premier League, and it does not look like being resolved anytime soon.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer: Chelsea forward "victim" of "sick" system, says PFA chief
Sports.text:
Cole Palmer is the "victim" of a "sick" system that is expecting too much of players, according to Professional Footballers' Association chief executive Maheta Molango.

Molango said Palmer's recent withdrawal from the England squad highlighted a match calendar that is unsustainable and has become the "survival of the fittest".

Five players – Palmer, Marcus Rashford, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento, external - pulled out of Thomas Tuchel's squad ahead of the latest international window.

"When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what's wrong about the industry?" Molango said at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

"You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?

"He's missing because he's a victim of the calendar and that's something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells."

The PFA and global players' union Fifpro have repeatedly warned about the impact of an increasingly congested calendar on player welfare.

In response to Palmer withdrawing from England's squad for "load management", Tuchel said the forward "misses too many opportunities", external .

But Molango criticised that stance, saying: "They [England players] love to play for England. They love to play for their national team. But unfortunately your body puts a limit to it. You cannot cheat biology."

Molango said this was far from an issue that only impacts England players, pointing to other recent withdrawals from European teams, including Germany's Kai Havertz, Dutch striker Brian Brobbey and France captain Kylian Mbappe.

"Is that really the football that we want?" Molango asked.

"Is it the football where the people who make us dream just cannot perform? For me it's very worrying.

"What we've seen over the last few years is a system that's sick, that's ill, because it ultimately revolves around obtaining votes and power consolidation."

Molango wants to see a mandatory three-week summer break and a three-week "retraining" period every summer.

While the Premier League's chief football officer, Rebecca Caplehorn, said she was supportive of this in theory, she said in practice it is not feasible at present.

"It's something we're really supportive of, conceptually, but the challenge is that it just doesn't fit into the current calendar," Caplehorn said.

"There's always something that's preventing us having that six-week gap that we want. Without regulatory change and change to the calendar, it's not possible for us to deliver that."

Sports.title: Brendan Venter: Saracens face fines after director of rugby refuses media commitments
Sports.text:
Saracens are set to receive a series of fines from Prem Rugby due to director of rugby Brendan Venter's failure to fulfil media commitments.

It is understood the club have already been handed a £5,000 sanction after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day.

The South African also did not speak to the media before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester.

The Daily Telegraph reported earlier on Tuesday, external that Venter "resigned" as director of rugby last month and took up a new role of "head of rugby culture and wine consultant", with head coach Joe Shaw assuming responsibility for media commitments.

The report also claims Saracens asked permission in July for Shaw to front the club's media commitments.

However, none of this has been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby.

It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities.

Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning to the club as director of rugby and have yet to confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities.

He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 trophy-laden years in the job.

Venter's first spell as Sarries' director of rugby, which began in 2009, also included clashes with authorities over media commitments.

In September 2010, the club apologised to European Rugby Cup (ERC) officials for then-captain Steve Borthwick's failure to attend the Heineken Cup launch at Cardiff's Millennium Stadium.

Borthwick, now England head coach, was the only missing representative from the coaches and captains of 12 English, Welsh and Scottish clubs attending the event.

He had been told by Saracens to instead attend a team bonding session at a beer festival in Munich.

In December 2010, Venter himself was warned by European Rugby Cup officials for a post-match interview after his side's 24-21 Heineken Cup loss to Racing Metro, in which he repeatedly gave short answers, agreeing with whatever was being asked.

He later said it was inspired by a scene in the football mockumentary film, Mike Bassett: England Manager.

Venter left his full-time role at Saracens halfway through the 2010–11 season, to be replaced by McCall.

Sports.title: Test cricket's biggest scandals: Rank BBC Sport's top 10
Sports.text:
Australia are due to play their first Test in South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal rocked the cricketing world eight years ago.

To mark one of the biggest controversies the game has ever seen, Test Match Special is asking which is Test cricket's biggest scandal.

Ten of the most famous scandals in Test cricket have been picked out by a TMS panel and we are asking you to rank them in order of how big they were.

Results of the vote will be revealed on the TMS podcast and you can read more about each scandal below the following vote.

On the 1932-33 tour of Australia, England needed a plan to stop the great Donald Bradman. Douglas Jardine, England's charismatic captain, came up with a tactic that would change the game forever: Bodyline.

Jardine instructed his fast bowlers, Harold Larwood and Bill Voce, to bowl hostile, short-pitched deliveries at the Australians. In an era when batters wore no upper-body protection, England's method was criticised as unsporting and against the spirit of cricket.

The bad blood between the two teams escalated to the administrators of the game in each country and even turned into a diplomatic incident, threatening to strain relationships between governments.

England won the series 4-1, a result almost lost in the infamy of the entire episode.

In 1968, England were due to tour South Africa, a country then operating under a system of racial segregation known as apartheid.

In line for selection was Basil D'Oliveira, a mixed-race all-rounder born in South Africa, who had emigrated to and qualified to play for England.

Despite scoring 158 in the final Test of the summer against Australia, D'Oliveira was initially left out of the England squad, only to then be called in as a replacement for the injured Tom Cartwright. His inclusion was criticised in South Africa and the tour was called off little more than a week later.

South Africa played one more Test series – at home to Australia the following year – then spent two decades out of international cricket. In the intervening time, a number of rebel tours to South Africa took place, with huge consequences for the players involved.

Australia were defending the Ashes in England in 1975. The series was shortened to four Tests because of the inaugural men's World Cup earlier in the summer.

At 1-0 down, England had a huge chance to level the series in the third Test at Headingley. At the close of the fourth day, Australia had reached 220-3 in pursuit of 445. A thrilling finish was in prospect.

Overnight, the pitch was vandalised. Holes were dug and oil was poured on the surface. The damage was caused by supporters of George Davis, who had been jailed for armed robbery the previous year. "George Davis is innocent" was written on the wall around the ground.

The Test was abandoned as a draw, meaning Australia retained the urn and ruining the prospect of a decider at The Oval.

Davis was released in 1976 when his conviction was adjudged to be unsafe, and it was overturned entirely on appeal in 2011.

In the mid-1970s, Kerry Packer, one of the richest men in Australia, wanted to boost the ratings of his Channel Nine TV network with live sport. He approached the Australian Cricket Board with a lucrative offer, one that was rejected in favour of keeping live cricket on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

So, Packer created his own product: World Series Cricket. The plan was simple – Packer recruited the best players in the world to stage his own matches.

Most significant was the signing of England captain Tony Greig, who effectively acted as an agent. Greig was stripped of the captaincy and Australia's 1977 Ashes tour of England was overshadowed by the emergence of Packer's outfit.

World Series Cricket lasted for two seasons – 1977-78 and 1978-79 – comprising one-day matches and 'SuperTests' between teams representing Australia, West Indies and a World XI. Meanwhile, traditional cricket rolled on. In 1978-79, England embarked on Ashes tour they won 5-1, beating an Australia side decimated by Packer defections.

Later in 1979, a truce between Packer and the board was brokered, and Nine earned TV rights to the game in Australia. Many of the innovations of WSC – coloured clothing and day-night cricket among them – shaped the game as we know it today.

England had already been frustrated by the decisions of a home umpire in losing the first Test on their tour of Pakistan in late 1987.

Shakoor Rana was appointed to stand in the second Test, much to England's displeasure. Rana had previously clashed with New Zealand skipper Jeremy Coney.

On the second day in Faisalabad, Rana was at square leg when he appeared to halt the game to object to one of England captain Mike Gatting's field placements.

Gatting was furious, confronting the official in footage that has been replayed over and over. The following day, Rana refused to take the field, leaving England waiting in the middle for play that did not get under way.

The match eventually resumed on the fourth day and the cancellation of the tour was narrowly avoided, but mistrust and ill-feeling between England and Pakistan lingered for years later.

In the mid-1990s, ball-tampering was the most emotive topic in Test cricket. In 1992, Pakistan's tour of England was overshadowed by allegations and innuendo. Two years later, the England captain found himself at the centre of a similar row.

In the Lord's Test against South Africa, Michael Atherton was caught by TV cameras rubbing dirt on the ball. Atherton's explanation was that he was trying to maintain the condition of the ball, rather than alter it. Trouble was, he told the match referee he was using the dirt to keep his hands dry.

The story was headline news, topped off by a chaotic news conference when Atherton was, in his own words, "fed to the lions". Atherton considered resigning, but escaped with a fine and remained captain for another four years.

Former South Africa captain Hansie Cronje was one of the most revered figures in his country. He was even close to Nelson Mandela.

Yet he became involved with Indian bookmakers and gradually made suggestions to fix matches, or parts of them. Cronje targeted impressionable team-mates to become part of his scheme.

Cronje's most infamous plot came in a dead-rubber fifth Test against England at Centurion Park in 2000. The match had been badly affected by rain, but Cronje was adamant the teams should do all they could to ensure it did not end in a draw.

He negotiated with England skipper Nasser Hussain for both teams to forfeit an innings, leaving the tourists with a final-day run-chase, which they completed. England were unaware, but Cronje had engineered a result.

Cronje confessed months later and would eventually give public testimony at the King Commission. He was banned from cricket for life and was killed in a plane crash in 2002.

No-balls deliberately bowled in the 2010 Lord's Test between England and Pakistan ultimately resulted in three of the tourists' players spending time in jail.

A sting by the News of the World newspaper paid a middleman - cricket agent Mazhar Majeed - for details of three no-balls.

Majeed arranged for Pakistan captain Salman Butt and pace bowlers Mohammad Asif and Mohammad Amir to execute the no-balls, then the News of the World broke the story while the Test was still ongoing.

All three players received bans from the International Cricket Council, then were found guilty of conspiracy to cheat at gambling and conspiracy to accept corrupt payments.

Butt was sentenced to two and a half years in prison, Asif a year and Amir, who was aged only 17 at the time of the no-ball plot, six months.

In the third Test of Australia's bad-tempered tour of South Africa in 2018, TV cameras picked up touring fielder Cameron Bancroft appearing to rub the ball with a small, yellow object.

Bancroft, along with captain Steve Smith, admitted to attempting to alter the condition of the ball. Days later, it was revealed Bancroft was using sandpaper.

The outcry engulfed the Australian team and the entire nation. Prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said he was "bitterly disappointed".

Smith was sacked, along with his vice-captain David Warner, the architect of the plot. All of Smith, Warner and Bancroft served lengthy bans from playing for Australia.

Coach Darren Lehmann was cleared of having knowledge of the ball-tampering, but he too resigned.

Sports.title: Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly miss out on latest Lionesses squad
Sports.text:
England manager Sarina Wiegman says Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly have "not been playing to their potential" and that is why they have missed out on selection.

The Lionesses face Greece in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off matches in October.

Manchester United midfielder Toone, 27, and Arsenal forward Kelly, 28 have had inconsistent starts to the season.

They both had crucial involvements at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025 as the Lionesses won back-to-back titles, but Wiegman is "convinced they can be better".

"Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"But that is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks.

"I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and of course, they want to work on that."

On reports suggesting Kelly's absence may have been linked to an injury, Wiegman added in her media conference: "I had the conversation with Chloe and for me, it was just what I saw on the pitch. I kept that with football with her."

In addition, Chelsea forward Aggie Beever-Jones and Arsenal duo Lotte Wubben-Moy and Taylor Hinds have not made the 23-player squad.

Captain Leah Williamson returns having missed June's 4-0 defeat by Spain and 3-0 win over Ukraine.

"I think she's played really well in the last few weeks and at the start of the season. She is happy and you can see," added Wiegman.

Meanwhile, there is a first senior call-up for Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter, 20, who has impressed alongside England's Keira Walsh in the Women's Super League.

She has started three of Chelsea's opening four matches and was a standout performer in their 1-0 win over Arsenal on Sunday.

"Her performances were just really good. We started following her closely last season and she got minutes over time," said Wiegman.

"She plays with a lot of courage, a lot of understanding and her decision-making is really good. Her technical ability, we have seen, is really good too.

"What I've seen is that no matter who she plays against, like last Sunday [against Arsenal], it looks like it doesn't bother her at all and she will just play football.

"She played against very high-level players, international players, and she just played. She looked very comfortable. I hope she shows that with us too."

There is also a return to the squad for uncapped midfielder Erica Meg Parkinson, 18, who has excelled since joining North Carolina Courage in the summer.

Manchester City full-back Niamh Charles made her return from injury as a substitute in their 1-0 win over Charlton Athletic on Saturday and is included.

London City Lionesses forward Freya Godfrey and Liverpool defender Grace Fisk are the other two uncapped players named.

England play a double-header against Greece, first in Crete on Friday, 9 October (17:30 BST) and then in Leicester on Tuesday, 13 October (19:30 BST).

If they win the two-legged tie, they progress to round two of the play-offs where they can compete for a place in next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

Sports.title: Liverpool: Inside the club's increasing global investment in youth
Sports.text:
Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but internally there is a realisation that after a significant amount of young talent was sold last summer, the club need to replenish that talent pool.

Since 2020, Liverpool have made more than £230m from selling players who have represented them at youth level and that has been a major part of owner Fenway Sports Group's self-sustaining business model, with the funds reinvested into the club.

Since Brexit, there is a 'premium' on young English players and it is why Liverpool's global talent department, led by Matt Newberry since the winter of 2024, now have a major role to play.

Fifa rules state that international transfers of players are only permitted if the player is over 18 and, since Brexit, Premier League clubs are no longer permitted to sign players under 18 from European countries.

Newberry's team is responsible for deciding which young talents from overseas should be targeted for a move. Using their wealth of contacts across the world, including dedicated regional scouts, Liverpool are becoming increasingly aggressive in the space.

It helps that new sporting director Julian Ward is well known for his global network.

"Any player we sign, the first intention is that we want them to play in the first team and there's a belief that there's a chance for everyone that signs here," Alex Inglethorpe, Liverpool Academy director told BBC Sport.

"That really is no different since the impact of Brexit on the English market, which is quite significant. There's now a premium on young English players. Time will tell if that premium is worthwhile but it's definitely a change.

"So it's fairly natural for a club like Liverpool to look within Merseyside in the first instance then broaden that out - national recruitment happens at 14 and after that you look globally, which is what we've done."

Mor Talla Ndiaye's journey began in the Senegalese village of Sandiara where he played football in the streets.

He progressed through the ranks playing for Bousports Academy in the town of Thiadiaye before joining Amitie Football Club in the city of Thies.

Come January this year, Liverpool fended off interest from other European clubs and signed the 18-year-old for about £1m plus add-ons.

"You have access to certain talent based on points accrued from playing homegrown players. We had a couple of ESC (elite significant contribution) spots to explore the wider market and that's something which, even prior to Brexit, was a fairly normal thing," Inglethorpe adds.

Ndiaye is a left-footed centre-half who played for Liverpool in pre-season under Andoni Iraola and was an unused substitute in three games in the second half of last season under Arne Slot.

"He's an incredible story, isn't he? From where he's come from to where he is - and he's such a humble kid. He's an unbelievable lad to work with," Rob Page, Liverpool's U21 boss, told BBC Sport.

"There's exciting times ahead but he's got a lot of work to do. He's nowhere near the finished article but he's on the right path. His attitude is spot on and he's at the club that will definitely help him develop."

At Liverpool, there is an optimism regarding Ndiaye and a genuine belief that if he makes it to the top, it could be one of the great football stories.

Liverpool opened discussions with his academy and his agency, Sport Cover, after scouts spotted his performances at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last winter and several video calls were arranged before the club's representatives travelled to Senegal.

Once there, they visited where Ndiaye trained, as well as meeting the people that supported his development before presenting their vision to him directly.

A round-table meeting was organised with his family to help understand his environment, the story and the context in which he grew up.

Ultimately, Ndiaye chose Liverpool because they offered the clearest pathway and their approach in getting to know him stood out.

Ndiaye isn't the only player to have been identified and recruited by Liverpool's global talent team.

After the U17 World Cup, Liverpool also made a £2.6m move for another centre-half, Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Ndukwe was impressive in pre-season and the 18-year-old Austrian has gone on loan to Levante in La Liga as he looks to obtain a UK work permit.

The list doesn't stop there. Samuel Martinez, the 17-year-old Colombian midfielder, will join next summer after having "30 offers from around the world, external", according to his father.

It doesn't always work. Arsenal beat Liverpool to the signing of Andria Bartishvili from Georgia last month and the 17-year-old will join the Gunners next summer when he is 18.

But the moves for Martinez and Ndiaye showcase Liverpool's willingness to spread beyond Europe and into areas they may not have explored before. Given the inevitability of other top clubs circling emerging talent, the idea of selling the pathway that Liverpool offers is imperative.

Since arriving, Ndiaye has settled in with a host family - which is normal when players aren't from the area - that are used to working with Liverpool.

"Players come from varying parts of the world and, when someone comes in and doesn't speak much English at the start, you have to help with that and help understand culturally the differences in food, the weather and even the pitches you play on," Inglethorpe said.

"There's a lot of understanding in terms of the level of support that's needed and the most important thing you can give a young player is the time.

"I'm delighted that Mor made such a strong impression and he's done as well as he has, but we hope that he's going to get better and better as he continues to adapt."

This summer, Liverpool also confirmed moves for Lucca Brughmans, the 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper, and Djylian N'Guessan, the 18-year-old French forward, with both set to join the club permanently in 2027.

In the modern game, most talents are known and there aren't many hidden gems anymore, but Liverpool believe that by digging deeper and wider they can get ahead of the curve, using their global network and their reputation as a club that will help players develop.

Sports.title: Fernando Alonso says 'I still feel as fast as anybody' as he confirms he will stay in F1 in 2027 with Aston Martin
Sports.text:
Fernando Alonso has committed to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year - and says the biggest single reason for his decision is because he "still feels fast".

The 45-year-old Spaniard has been weighing up his future all year. And while, like Max Verstappen, he has been outspoken in his criticism of the new hybrid engines introduced in 2026, his love for the sport has won out.

"First, this is my life," Alonso told BBC Sport in his only English language interview about his decision, which was announced on Tuesday., external

"I have this in my blood and I keep racing and I keep enjoying and this is a way of life, in a way.

"Probably for me the biggest, or the clearest thing to keep racing is I still feel self-confidence that I have something extra.

"And when I think about stepping down or taking a different role in the team or not driving the car or whatever, in a way I feel it should not be like that because I still feel as fast as anybody. So let's have another go."

His own personal performance was only one factor at play in Alonso's decision, he explained in an extensive and open conversation.

Alonso also considered the new rules, and the competitiveness of his team, which has been close to rock bottom for most of this season.

Alonso is regarded as one of the all-time F1 greats, and has created an iconic status over a career that dates back to 2001.

And he continues to reject any suggestion that he has lost any of his ability.

"When I jump in the car, in free practice, I will see some people braking late in a corner, locking up the front tyres here or there, making mistakes there," Alonso says.

"I feel that I'm OK. Or, I'm faster than them.

"So when I get changed and I go back home, even if I'm P18, in a way I feel some satisfaction and pride inside, even if it should not be the case because we are not competitive.

"How will I be in the living room, watching TV, thinking that I can do better? That will be my feeling now. When that changes, if I see that I lost abilities, I lost speed, I lost reflexes, I lost something, then I will be happy to watch from my living room the race.

"At the moment, I feel it was not the time because I'm better than that guy. I'm better than that other guy. I will think like that. And I cannot stop racing if I still think like that."

Alonso has only had a couple of chances this year to prove his point that he's still as good as he ever was. One was at the Dutch Grand Prix, when he finished ninth, holding at bay the faster cars of Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

I suggest to him that it was a typical Alonso drive, proof to those who doubted that he still has it. But he says it will have had no impact on the audience.

"You only prove to people when you are in the podium or you are on TV," he says. "That's where eyes are open, and people remember suddenly that you're still on the grid.

"So now I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous, and no one knows that we're still there and we're still fast.

"We are preparing ourselves for the moment of truth and that will be a surprise for everybody again."

Along with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Alonso has been one of the drivers most critical of the 2026 rules.

Drivers feel the new hybrid engines, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have diminished F1's challenge.

The key problems are the fact the cars run out of half their energy long before some corners, a process known as "derating", and that some of the sport's most demanding corners have been neutered because they are used to charge the batteries.

Alonso, as is his way, has produced some particularly pithy turns of phrase this season to express his unhappiness.

He has called F1 the "battery world championship". He has described fast corners as "the charging station for the car" and said that "the chef could drive the car" in a particular corner in Bahrain that used to be a major challenge.

And he's been dismissive of the increased number of overtaking moves created by offsets in energy levels between cars, calling them "avoidance actions".

How did he square all that with deciding to keep racing these cars he dislikes so much?

"That's a good question," he says, "because that was the hardest thing for me."

He says he hopes the changes being made to change the power ratio to 60-40 in two steps by 2028 "will make things a little bit easier".

"This year, there have been some good races and some bad races," Alonso says. "Maybe some of the shorter circuits that you had the battery until the braking point are changing the way you perceive the driving.

"And some of the circuits like Silverstone, Spa, Suzuka, they were very bad, you know, because they derate and things like that.

"Maybe even for next year they can tweak a little bit the battery power to have a little bit maybe less battery for longer or something like that because F1 at the moment is not natural driving.

"Reaching the top speed in the middle of the straight, it goes against the driver instinct of braking late and going on power earlier. It seems that if you want to drive these cars fast, you ended up going slower and that's not the way it should be."

Alonso says that, as something of an elder statesman, he "feels some responsibility also in this regard to help the sport" make the right decisions for the future.

And the willingness of governing body the FIA and commercial rights holder F1 to accept there is a problem and make changes to address it has also been a reassurance.

"It does help that the sport keeps chasing ideas and talking to the drivers and the teams (about) how to make things better, even for the next set of regulations," he says.

"This gives me also some hope that I will enjoy more the driving next year than I did this year."

It has been a dismal year for Aston Martin, whose car has been uncompetitive, while Honda's engine has been the worst in the field on the Japanese manufacturer's official return to F1.

But a massive update to the car for the Hungarian Grand Prix cut something like two seconds off lap times, offering hope for next season.

A key influence in Alonso's decision was Adrian Newey, whose arrival as managing technical partner in March 2025 delayed the start of work on this year's car, the first of a cascading series of issues that led to this year's performance.

Alonso has been waiting his entire career to work with the man regarded as the greatest technical mind of his generation, perhaps ever. So giving up after just one, highly compromised, year together felt senseless.

"This team has all the ingredients to have success in the future," Alonso says, "and I didn't feel that this was the moment to leave. It was the moment to keep on going, giving a second chance to Honda as well to fix their problems as well and stay together with the team.

"Adrian was probably the biggest contributor to this. We didn't start it right this year but things are moving in the right direction and he's capable of changing things very quickly.

"Aston is my family. I know Lawrence (Stroll, the owner) and Lance (Stroll, Alonso's team-mate) for many, many years. We keep open conversations, many different topics, every week. And that will be the case also for next year."

Honda's engine upgrade, which debuted at the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August, was not especially convincing.

Alonso has bad memories of Honda from his time with McLaren from 2015-17, and he admits living through a similar experience again "has been difficult".

But major steps have been taken to address the internal issues at the company and Alonso says: "They are moving in the right direction. There are no guarantees that next year the engine will be completely fixed but all the changes that are happening in Honda made sense, so I have faith.

"The trust that I have in the team, it didn't change even throughout this difficult year. In the future, I don't know how long it's going to take, but it will be a successful team, and I want to be part of it."

There was one final factor - family. Alonso became a father this year when his partner, the Spanish television presenter Melissa Jimenez, gave birth to their son, Leonard, in March.

Has that had any effect on his approach to life and his career?

"I would say not," Alonso says. "I was (initially) thinking yes, and I tried to think about, family first, what will be the best for my son next year if I have this tight calendar or not and things like that.

"But then quickly I realised that it was not really a key factor. This year it was difficult for him to travel; he's only six months old now. But I think next year he will come to 50% of the races or more.

"So I could even enjoy my life more, travelling around the world with my son. That's a huge privilege that I will hopefully enjoy next year.

"Racing next year, it was my natural, final decision. I will be racing in any car, even when I stop Formula 1, but F1 is still in my blood.

"One more year made all the sense in the world for now."

Or, he hints, perhaps longer:

"I see that it would not be only one year, but I don't have any pressure to think about it."

Sports.title: Why Salisbury FC are 'bigger than many Premier League teams' in Kuwait
Sports.text:
As with every home game, the Salisbury FC players and coaching staff went to embrace the fans in the Andrews Terrace at The Ray Mac Stadium after Saturday's 2-0 win against Folkestone Invicta.

Alongside the normal applause and cheers, they were greeted with a chant that isn't a regular from the songbook.

"Kuwait away ole, ole," sang fans of the National League South outfit.

The players clapped back with an extra buzz - within 24 hours they would be travelling to the Middle East.

"Straight away we all said, 'yeah, we're all in," explains Salisbury player Luke Russe.

"It's a unique opportunity and as players, we are so thankful to everybody involved in making this trip happen. I've been involved in this level for a long time now and I've never had an experience like it."

The five-day trip involves the club facing one of Kuwait's most successful teams on Wednesday, Al Qadsia, who have won more than 50 trophies, before returning on Thursday to play Saturday's FA Cup third qualifying round against Dulwich Hamlet.

It comes as part of the club's continued link with Kuwait through their owner Ali Alhamad, who purchased the club in 2025.

The club hopes the trip will offer significant commercial growth and, for the players, an opportunity to experience football in a new environment and culture.

The Mohammad Al-Hamad Stadium holds 22,000 spectators, more than five times that of Salisbury's The Ray Mac.

"We'd love to win the game," says Russe. "But at the same time I think it's more about the experience and about the club as a whole, going over there, living that way of life and experiencing the game.

"We've got a very young group, so for them to experience that and kind of experience cultures and differences is great.

"It'll be a fantastic opportunity for us players, for the staff, and I think it'll bring the whole club even closer to what we are now."

The players will get to visit local restaurants, try local food and coffee, visit schools and universities, and hold a question and answer session for locals to understand how an English football club operates from the perspective of owner Alhamad.

"It will help the players themselves with opening up their horizons into different cultures, different countries, experiencing other footballing nations and other styles of football," he says.

The country's interest in Salisbury is evident.

Four of the club's sponsors are from Kuwait, including the front of shirt sponsor for a company that created the country's first Sharia-compliant digital bank, and the training kit represents a popular Acai company that can only be bought in Kuwait.

On Instagram the official Arabic account of Salisbury FC has more than 14,000 followers - only slightly fewer than their official English profile.

When the squad arrived in Kuwait they were greeted by a small group of fans, while school children interacted with them as if they were Premier League players.

"I would even go further than saying that Salisbury in Kuwait is bigger than many of the Premier League teams in the UK," says Alhamad.

"So I am not exaggerating when I do say that it is a huge name in Kuwait but what's more important than the size is we are contributing a lot to the local community here in Kuwait and to the children and the future of the football in Kuwait.

"Salisbury really is an integral part of opening those avenues and helping the youth here to be better in all the aspects we're looking for."

The eagerness the players showed shocked Alhamad, with all of the squad, except Jaiden Bartolo who is on international duty, agreeing to go within an hour.

Along with the cultural experience, the club is also using this as a way to grow financially, with all ticket sales and advertisement money going to Salisbury.

Meanwhile, Salisbury have set up a summer camp in the country and ran a trial session where the top three players trained with the first team during pre-season.

"It's quite simple in my mind. If you do what other people do, you'll just get the same results everyone else does," says Alhamad.

"Football in England, especially in the non-league, is a brutal business. So just throwing in money to the football club with the aim of getting promotion is fool's gold, in my opinion.

"The right way to do it is to build it properly all the way from the bottom and if you just limit yourself to one market, which is the city or town that you are in, that is pretty limited.

"With social media and the avenues we have, such as being in Kuwait and the Gulf and Arab regions. That's a huge untapped market that is thirsty for English football."

People in Kuwait are avid watchers of the Premier League but non-league is still very much an unknown commodity in the country.

"People are not properly educated in the fact that the non-league is actually a really high quality and that is also an indirect goal of mine with this match," he adds.

"We're here to show them, you're belittling, playing the sixth tier of English football, the second step of the English non-league.

"We'll show you what we have and you never know, maybe the sixth tier of English football will beat the top tier on the biggest team in Kuwait.

"That'll be some story."
